title: Dec 2018 (Set 2)
subtitle: Verified Answer Key (100/100 Qs) + Crisp Simple-English Explanations

items.title: Q1 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Geoffrey Chaucer, William Shakespeare
items.stem:
What is peculiar about the reference in the following to some poets’ names in the plural ?
“It is a freezing, bleak day in January, and I am looking for poetry. I see a few Chaucers, a few Shakespeares, and a hardcover, three-dollar History of Modern Poetry published in 1987.”
options: Unusual; awkward metaphors no longer in use.
Synecdochic use; names for their respective works.
Standard reference to more texts of one poet/author.
Usually refer to biographies of the poets in question.
items.explanation: Here the poets' names stand for their books (copies of Chaucer and Shakespeare). Using a name for the author's works is a figure of speech, closely related to metonymy.

items.title: Q2 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit II: Poetry · John Donne
options: Distress comes in many forms, but none lasts as long as heartache.
Love tends to grab us and never let go.
Unbidden pain afflicts us, but we are lured by love.
Emotions can damage us, but none as severely as love.
items.explanation: Line 5 says other griefs simply come to us, but love draws us in. So pain arrives on its own, while love attracts us.

items.title: Q3 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem: Which of the following acts were not passed during the Victorian Era ?
options: The Married Women’s Property Rights Act
items.explanation: Factory Acts, custody-of-infants laws and the Married Women's Property Acts were passed in Victoria's reign. Women's suffrage was granted only in 1918, after the Victorian era.

items.title: Q4 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit II: Poetry · Samuel Johnson
items.stem: In imitation of which classical poet did Samuel Johnson write his London and The Vanity of Human Wishes ?
items.explanation: Johnson's London imitates Juvenal's Third Satire, and The Vanity of Human Wishes imitates Juvenal's Tenth Satire.

items.title: Q5 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Samuel Beckett
items.stem:
Match the plays to their setting :
(a) Krapp’s Last Tape  (i) A country road; A tree.
(b) Happy Days  (ii) Bare interior; Two small windows high up; grey light.
(c) Waiting for Godot  (iii) Expanse of scorched grass forming a low mound; blinding light.
(d) Endgame  (iv) A late evening in future; white light.
items.explanation: Krapp's room is set on 'a late evening in the future', Happy Days on a scorched mound, Godot on a country road with a tree, and Endgame in a bare interior with high windows.

items.title: Q6 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Early Tudor & Humanist Reformation · Unit II: Poetry · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: One of the less noticed and acknowledged distinction of The Canterbury Tales is that
options: it upheld the idea that we cannot divorce poetry from knowledge because poetry itself is an object of knowledge.
it alerted us to the term auctor, someone who is both ‘an originator, or one who gives increase’, the best description for Chaucer himself.
instead of revealing England’s divisions, it revelled in its diversity.
it married domesticity to divinity, the baker’s loaf with the bread of life.
items.explanation: Chaucer's work brought the idea of the 'auctor' (originator, one who gives increase) into English, and it fits Chaucer himself.

items.title: Q7 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · John Keats
items.stem: Which interpretation of Keats’s “Beauty is truth, truth beauty” best represents the mimetic perspective ?
options: The author’s arbitrary imposition of order upon the chaotic impressions of reality constitutes the only “truth” in a work of art.

The line is an ironic quotation, the equation of “beauty” and “truth” as “all we know on earth” suggests that reality is an illusory concept and that the primary function of art is to construct a world within an aesthetic reality of its own.

Those aspects of reality which we perceive to be “beautiful” are the only worthy subject matter of the artist, and it is the artist’s job to observe closely and isolate those sublime elements from the flux of the mundane.
A work of literature is “beautiful” insofar as it offers an accurate representation of its subject matter, with fully realized characters and vivid description of events.
items.explanation: The mimetic view judges art by how truly it imitates reality. So literature is 'beautiful' when it represents its subject accurately.

items.title: Q8 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · John Keats
items.stem:
Match the poem with the opening lines :
(a) “Ode to Psyche”  (i) “My heart aches, and a drowsy numbness pains / My sense, as though of hemlock I had drunk,”
(b) “Ode on a Grecian Urn”  (ii) “No, no, go not to Lethe, neither twist / Wolf’s-bane, tight-rooted, for its poisonous wine,”
(c) “Ode to a Nightingale”  (iii) “Thou still unravish’d bride of quietness, / Thou foster-child of silence and slow time,”
(d) “Ode on Melancholy”  (iv) “O Goddess ! hear these tuneless numbers, wrung / By sweet enforcement and remembrance dear,”
items.explanation: 'O Goddess! hear these tuneless numbers' opens Psyche, 'Thou still unravish'd bride' opens the Urn, 'My heart aches' opens the Nightingale, and 'No, no, go not to Lethe' opens Melancholy.

items.title: Q9 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII
items.stem:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Read the statements and choose the correct answer using the code given below :
Assertion (A) : Gender studies do not see an urgent need to help us navigate the various pitfalls of racism, ethnocentrism, cultural relativism, and plain ignorance that flow from using “culture” as an explanatory tool.
Reason (R) : Issues relating to women’s rights, gender roles, sexuality and family obligations are centrally implicated in the so-called clash of civilizations between Christianity or Secularism, and Islam.
items.explanation: Assertion (A) claims gender studies see no urgent need, while (R) shows gender issues are central to cultural clashes, which argues the opposite. So (R) does not follow from (A).

items.title: Q10 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Roland Barthes
items.stem:
“We know now that a text is not a line of words releasing a single “theological” meaning (the “message” of the Author-God) but a multidimensional space in which a variety of writings, none of them original, blend and clash. . . . Literature . . . by refusing to assign a “secret”, an ultimate meaning, to the text (and to the world as text) liberates what may be called an anti-theological activity, an activity that is truly revolutionary since to refuse to fix meaning is, in the end to refuse God and his hypostases – reason, science, law.”
The passage comes from which of the following essays ?
options: “Tradition and Individual Talent” by T.S. Eliot
“The Death of the Author” by Roland Barthes
“What is an Author ?” by Michel Foucault
“Discourse in the Novel” by Mikhail Bakhtin
items.explanation: The 'Author-God' and the text as 'a multidimensional space' are from Roland Barthes' 'The Death of the Author' (1967).

items.title: Q11 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem:
Match the following concepts with their definitions :
(Concepts) (Definitions)
(a) Collocation  (i) A semantic relationship of one-to-many
(b) Corpus  (ii) A grid used in lexical analysis
(c) Hyponymy  (iii) A combination of two lexical items in a grammatical pattern
(d) Matrix  (iv) A large body of texts
items.explanation: Collocation is a lexical pairing in a grammatical pattern, a corpus is a large body of texts, hyponymy is a one-to-many sense relation, and a matrix is a grid for lexical analysis.

items.title: Q12 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Thomas De Quincey
items.stem:
The Romantic period produced a fair amount of dramatic criticism. A notable example is “On the Knocking at the Gate in Macbeth.”
Who is the author ?
items.explanation: Thomas De Quincey wrote 'On the Knocking at the Gate in Macbeth' (1823). Kean and Macready were actors, not essayists.

items.title: Q13 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Francis Bacon
items.stem:
“Search the heads of the greatest rivers in the world, you shall find them but bubbles of water.”
Who is the author of this line ?
items.explanation: The line is attributed to Francis Bacon and reflects his aphoristic prose style.

items.title: Q14 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · D.H. Lawrence
items.stem:
Match the character with the work :
(Characters) (Name of work)
(a) Rupert Birkin  (i) Sons and Lovers
(b) Lydia Lensky  (ii) Kangaroo
(c) Miriam Leivers  (iii) Women in Love
(d) Richard Somers  (iv) The Rainbow
items.explanation: Birkin is in Women in Love, Lydia Lensky in The Rainbow, Miriam Leivers in Sons and Lovers, and Richard Somers in Kangaroo. All are novels by D.H. Lawrence.

items.title: Q15 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Graham Swift
items.stem:
“Reality is that nothing happens. How many of the events of history have occurred, ask yourselves, for this and for that reason, but for no other reason, fundamentally, than the desire to make things happen ? I present to you History, the fabrication, the diversion, the reality-obscuring drama.”
Which postmodern novel thus subverts the truth claims of traditional historiography ?
options: John Fowles’s The French Lieutenant’s Woman
items.explanation: This is the history teacher Tom Crick's speech in Graham Swift's Waterland (1983), a classic of historiographic metafiction.

items.title: Q16 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Arnold Wesker
items.stem:
Arnold Wesker is associated with “kitchen-sink drama”, a rather condescending title applied to the then new-wave realistic drama depicting the family lives of working-class characters, on stage and in broadcast plays. Two of the following plays begin with one character doing the dishes in a kitchen sink. Identify the pair.
(i) The Kitchen
(ii) Chicken Soup with Barley
(iii) Roots
(iv) Menace
The right combination according to the code is :
items.explanation: Chicken Soup with Barley and Roots (parts of Wesker's Trilogy) open in domestic kitchens. The Kitchen is set in a restaurant kitchen and Menace is a television play. Marked doubtful.

items.title: Q17 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit II: Poetry · Federico García Lorca
items.stem: The titular figure of Federico García Lorca’s elegy “Lament for Ignacio Sánchez Mejías” was
options: a revolutionary who was associated with Che Guevara
a spy who helped the revolutionaries during the Spanish Civil War
items.explanation: Ignacio Sánchez Mejías was a famous bullfighter, and also a writer and Lorca's friend. He was gored in 1934, and Lorca wrote the elegy for him.

items.title: Q18 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Tobias Smollett
items.stem: Which of the following is not indebted to the Gothic genre ?
items.explanation: Vathek, The Monk and The Italian are Gothic novels. Smollett's Roderick Random is a picaresque adventure novel.

items.title: Q19 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: The en-ending to denote the plural nous (as in oxen, children, brethren) has survived from the
options: Old English practice of making plural nouns
Anglo-Norman case of making plural nouns
Odd Middle-English pronouncing custom of plurals
Middle English hymnals and chants in English parishes
items.explanation: The -en plural comes from Old English weak noun endings, and only a few forms like oxen survive today.

items.title: Q20 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
“Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow,
________ in this petty pace from day to day,
To the last ________ of recorded time;
And all our yesterdays have lighted fools
The way to dusty death. Out, out, brief candle !
Life’s but a walking shadow, a poor player,
That ________ and frets his hour upon the stage,
And then is ________ no more: it is a tale
Told by an idiot, full of sound and fury,
Signifying nothing.”
Fill in the blanks. Choose the set that carries the correct words.
items.explanation: Macbeth's lines read 'Creeps in this petty pace', 'last syllable of recorded time', 'struts and frets his hour', and 'is heard no more'.

items.title: Q21 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Restoration Age (Age of Dryden) · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · George Etherege, William Wycherley, John Marston
items.stem:
Match the Character with the Play :
(Character) (Play)
(a) Dorimant  (i) The Plain Dealer
(b) Lady Fidget  (ii) The Man of Mode
(c) Malevole  (iii) The Country Wife
(d) Vernish  (iv) The Malcontent
items.explanation: Dorimant is in Etherege's The Man of Mode, Lady Fidget in Wycherley's The Country Wife, Malevole in Marston's The Malcontent, and Vernish in Wycherley's The Plain Dealer.

items.title: Q22 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Italo Calvino
items.stem: In which of his novels does Italo Calvino construct his narrative through a tarot pack of cards and re-interpret the Western canon providing new versions of Oedipus Rex, Faust, Hamlet, Macbeth and King Lear ?
options: The Path to the Nest of Spiders
items.explanation: In The Castle of Crossed Destinies (1969) travellers tell stories by laying out tarot cards, which retell Oedipus, Faust, Hamlet and other classics.

items.title: Q23 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Edwardian, Georgian & Irish Literary Revival · Unit II: Poetry · Rudyard Kipling
items.stem:
During the Raj, the British viewed their rule in terms of a thankless duty to uplift the downtrodden and inculcate order into Oriental minds. The mission to civilize the “silent, sullen peoples” of the East was a burden imposed upon them by destiny.
The last observation is a fairly obvious allusion to
options: Maud Diver’s The Englishwoman in India
J.R. Ackerley’s Hindoo Holiday : An Indian Journal
Flora Annie Steel’s “The Garden of Fidelity”
items.explanation: 'Silent, sullen peoples' is a phrase from Kipling's 'The White Man's Burden' (1899), the poem about the imperial 'civilising mission'.

items.title: Q24 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Parallel 19th-C Tracks: American Renaissance, Realism & Early Indian English · Unit II: Poetry · William Cullen Bryant, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, Oliver Wendell Holmes
items.stem: Identify the Fireside poets of the US.
options: William Cullen Bryant, H.W. Longfellow, Oliver Wendell Holmes
T.S. Eliot, Wallace Stevens, William Carlos Williams
Amy Lowell, Emily Dickinson, Phillis Wheatley
Marianne Moore, Elizabeth Bishop, Anne Seaton
items.explanation: The Fireside Poets were popular nineteenth-century New England poets: Bryant, Longfellow, Holmes, Whittier and Lowell.

items.title: Q25 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Christopher Marlowe
items.stem:
In Marlow’s Doctor Faustus, what books does Valdes counsel Faustus to study in preparation for conjuring up spirits ?
(i) The works of Bacon and Abanus
(ii) The Hebrew Psalter and New Testament
(iii) The works of Ovid and Homer
(iv) The works of Baxter and Horst
The right combination according to the code is :
items.explanation: Valdes tells Faustus to study 'Albanus' works, the Hebrew Psalter and New Testament' (Roger Bacon and Albanus) for conjuring.

items.title: Q26 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Wolfgang Iser
items.stem: What is an “implied reader” ?
options: The ideal audience envisioned by the author and to whom the work of literature is supposedly addressed.
A reader who embodies all those predispositions necessary for a literary work to exercise its effect.
The ideal “average” reader who can approach a work of literature with no preconceived ideas about the author’s life, the time of composition, etc.
The ideal reader of a work of literature which is approximated over time by successive responses of generations of actual readers.
items.explanation: Wolfgang Iser's implied reader is the role built into the text, embodying the predispositions needed for the work to have its effect.

items.title: Q27 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Horace
items.stem: Who among the ancients prescribed that poetry should both instruct and delight ?
items.explanation: Horace in the Ars Poetica said poets aim 'to instruct or to delight, or to combine both' (utile et dulce).

items.title: Q28 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Chitra Banerjee Divakaruni, Anita Rau Badami, Anjana Appachana, Indira Ganesan
items.stem:
Match the following authors with the novels :
(Name of Author) (Name of Novel)
(a) Chitra Banerjee Divakaruni  (i) Inheritance
(b) Anita Rau Badami  (ii) Listening Now
(c) Anjana Appachana  (iii) Sister of My Heart
(d) Indira Ganesan  (iv) The Hero’s Walk
items.explanation: Divakaruni wrote Sister of My Heart, Badami The Hero's Walk, Appachana Listening Now, and Ganesan Inheritance.

items.title: Q29 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · I.A. Richards
items.stem: In his Practical Criticism I.A. Richards suggests that there are several kinds of meanings and that the “total meaning” is a blend of contributory meanings which are of different types. He identified four kinds of meaning, or the total meaning of a word depends upon four factors. Choose the right combination as proposed by Richards.
items.explanation: Richards' four kinds of meaning are Sense, Feeling, Tone and Intention.

items.title: Q30 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Caroline & Commonwealth / Puritan Interregnum · Unit II: Poetry · Thomas Carew, Richard Lovelace, Robert Herrick
items.stem: Which of the following themes was not common to the works of Cavalier poets such as Thomas Carew, Sir John Denham, Edmund Waller, Sir John Suckling, James Shirley, Richard Lovelace, and Robert Herrick ?
options: Courtly ideals of the good life
items.explanation: Cavalier poetry is about courtly life, carpe diem and royalist loyalty. Pious devotion is typical of the Metaphysical religious poets instead.

items.title: Q31 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · William Blake
items.stem: In which work does William Blake say that Milton was “a true poet and of devil’s party without knowing it” ?
items.explanation: The remark about Milton being 'of the Devil's party without knowing it' is in Blake's The Marriage of Heaven and Hell.

items.title: Q32 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit II: Poetry · Alfred Tennyson, Walt Whitman, Rudyard Kipling
items.stem: What attitude towards death would you find in such poems as Tennyson’s “Crossing the Bar,” Whitman’s “Death Carol,” and Kipling’s “L’Envoi” ?
items.explanation: These poems face death calmly and accept it rather than fear or fight it. Marked doubtful because 'Hope' could also be argued.

items.title: Q33 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Parallel Modernist Tracks: American Modernism, Harlem Renaissance & Indian Gandhian Era · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · W.E.B. Du Bois
items.stem: Which of the following is the most accurate statement by W.E.B. Du Bois’s famous articulation of the ‘twoness’ of black Americans ?
options: “This sense of always looking at one’s self, a peculiar sensation through the eyes of others, is double consciousness.”
“It is a peculiar sensation, this double-consciousness, this sense of always looking at one’s self through the eyes of others.”
“Through the eyes of others, this sense of always looking at one’s self, we acquire the double-consciousness.”
“This double consciousness, this sense of always looking at one’s self through the eyes of others, is a peculiar sensation.”
items.explanation: In The Souls of Black Folk Du Bois wrote: 'It is a peculiar sensation, this double-consciousness, this sense of always looking at one's self through the eyes of others.'

items.title: Q34 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Charles Dickens
items.stem: Nicholas Nickleby firmly established Charles Dickens as a dominant novelist of his time and the book as an unrivalled literary phenomenon. To celebrate the completion of the book, a painter noted that there had been nothing comparable to him since the days of Samuel Richardson. Identify the painter.
items.explanation: The painter is usually named as Sir David Wilkie, a Scottish artist who admired Dickens.

items.title: Q35 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Jacques Derrida
items.stem: Deconstructionist critics argue that texts are never free from
options: the equivocal and ironically unstable worldview of the author.
the material conditions that determine the production and reception.
distortions inherent in the rhetoricity of language.
the interpretations bestowed by the totalizing critic.
items.explanation: Deconstruction holds that language is figurative and unstable, so every text carries distortions from its own rhetoric.

items.title: Q36 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
“Full many a lady
I have eye’d with best regard: and many a time
The harmony of their tongues hath into bondage
Brought my too diligent ear; for several virtues
Have I liked several women; never any
With so full soul, but some defect in her
Did quarrel with the noblest grace she ow’d,
And put it to the foil. But you, O you,
So perfect and so peerless, are created
Of every creature’s best.”
This passage admiring the perfect matching of inner and outward beauty of a woman is taken from
options: John Webster’s The Duchess of Malfi
items.explanation: This is Ferdinand's speech to Miranda in The Tempest (Act 3, Scene 1).

items.title: Q37 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy · Adrian Holliday
items.stem: In traditional ELT methods and materials, the native speaker is elevated and idealized against stereotyped non-native speakers. This tendency is dubbed ________ by Adrian Holliday.
items.explanation: Adrian Holliday coined 'native-speakerism' for the belief that native speakers are the ideal teachers and models.

items.title: Q38 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Augustan Age (Age of Pope & Swift) · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Daniel Defoe, Albert Camus
items.stem:
Albert Camus borrows the following epigraph to his novel The Plague from ________.
“It is as reasonable to represent one kind of imprisonment by another, as it is to represent anything that really exists by that which exists not.”
options: Jeremy Bentham’s The Principles of Morals and Legislation
James Hogg’s The Confessions of a Justified Sinner
Robert Burton’s The Anatomy of Melancholy
items.explanation: Camus took the epigraph of The Plague from Defoe, written in the preface to Robinson Crusoe.

items.title: Q39 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · W.B. Yeats, Rabindranath Tagore
items.stem:
I have carried the manuscript of these translations about with me for days, reading it in railway trains, or on the top of omnibuses and in restaurants, and I have often had to close it lest some stranger would see how much it moved me. These lyrics — which are in the original, my ... (Indian friends) tell me, full of subtlety of rhythm, of untranslatable delicacies of colour, of metrical invention — display in their thought a world I have dreamed of all my life long. The work of a supreme culture, they yet appear as much a growth of the common soil as the grass and the rushes. A tradition, where poetry and religion are the same thing, has passed through the centuries, gathering from learned and unlearned metaphor and emotion, and carried back again to the multitude the thought of the scholar and the noble. If the civilization of Bengal remains unbroken, if that common mind which — as one divines — runs through all, is not, as with us, broken into a dozen minds that know nothing of each other, something even of what is most subtle in these verses will have come, in a few generations, to the beggar on the roads.
—W.B. Yeats, from Introduction to Rabindranath Tagore’s Gitanjali
In this passage, Yeats praises Indian culture primarily because it
options: is accessible to Westerners though it is rooted in a different religious tradition.
reflects a marvellous eclecticism in drawing from many disparate cultures.
has been flexible enough to survive a transition into the modern world.
embodies values and gives rise to art that can be shared by people of all classes.
items.explanation: Yeats stresses that Bengal's poetry passes from scholars and nobles to beggars on the road, a shared culture across all classes.

items.title: Q40 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit II: Poetry · Rudyard Kipling
items.stem:
The following epitaph was written by Rudyard Kipling during the War of 1914 – 18.
HINDU SEPOY IN FRANCE
This man in his own country prayed we know not to what Powers.
We pray Them to reward him for his bravery in ours.
“Powers” here refers to ________, “Them” to ________, and “ours” to ________.
options: the Hindus, the French, the British
the military, the Hindu sepoys, Powers
items.explanation: 'Powers' means the divine beings the sepoy prayed to, 'Them' repeats Powers, and 'ours' is the speaker's country (France/Britain's side).

items.title: Q41 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Francis Jeffrey
items.stem: Who viewed Wordsworth, Southey and Coleridge as representatives of a “sect of poets ... dissenters from the established systems in poetry and criticism” who constituted “the most formidable conspiracy against sound judgement in matters political” ?
items.explanation: Francis Jeffrey, editor of the Edinburgh Review, attacked the Lake Poets in his reviews.

items.title: Q42 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Caroline & Commonwealth / Puritan Interregnum · Unit II: Poetry · John Milton
items.stem:
Alas ! what boots it with uncessant care
To tend the homely, slighted Shepherd’s trade,
And strictly meditate the thankless Muse ?
Were it not better done, as others use,
To sport with Amaryllis in the shade,
Or with the tangles of Neaera’s hair ?
Who are Amaryllis and Neaera in the above extract from John Milton’s “Lycidas” ?
options: Both were one-time lovers of Lycidas, the dead shepherd.
Amaryllis is a shepherdess mentioned in ancient pastoral poetry, notably in Virgil’s Eclogues; Neaera, a nymph who appears in Virgil’s Eclogues.
Both were goddesses of love and war respectively appearing in Greek pastoral poetry.
Amaryllis is a shepherdess mentioned in Shakespeare’s romantic comedies; Neaera, a minor character in Love’s Labour’s Lost.
items.explanation: Amaryllis and Neaera are stock pastoral names from classical poetry, especially Virgil's Eclogues.

items.title: Q43 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Caroline & Commonwealth / Puritan Interregnum · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Gerrard Winstanley
items.stem: The term ‘Digger’ is associated with a group of agrarian communists who flourished in England in 1649 – 50 and were led by
items.explanation: Gerrard Winstanley led the Diggers, who farmed common land in 1649–50. Lilburne led the Levellers and Fox the Quakers.

items.title: Q44 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Early Tudor & Humanist Reformation · Unit II: Poetry · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem:
One of the most flexible metres, ________ is a five foot line. It was introduced by Geoffrey Chaucer in the fourteenth century and has since then become the commonest of metres in English poetry.
(Fill in the blank)
items.explanation: A pentameter has five feet, and Chaucer introduced the iambic pentameter line to English.

items.title: Q45 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Plato
items.stem: Why did Plato banish the poet from his ideal state ?
options: Poetry makes an artificial distinction between form and content.
Poetry deals with form, to the neglect of content.
In representing the sensual aspects of reality, the poet fails to discern the transcendent reality behind mere appearance.
The poet can never produce a completely accurate replica of the reality it seeks to represent, and (moreover) the purpose of art is not to describe reality but to change it.
items.explanation: For Plato poetry imitates the world of appearances, which is itself a copy of the real Forms, so the poet is twice removed from truth.

items.title: Q46 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Samuel Johnson
items.stem:
The fault of Cowley and perhaps of all the writers of the metaphysical race is that of pursuing his thoughts to their ramifications, by which he loses the grandeur of generality; for of the greatest things the parts are little; what is little can be but pretty, and by claiming dignity becomes ridiculous. Thus all the power of description is destroyed by a scrupulous enumeration; and the force of metaphors is lost, when the mind by the mention of particulars is turned more upon the original than the secondary sense, more upon that from which the illustration is drawn than that to which it is applied.
(Life of Cowley, 1779)
What Dr. Johnson actually faults here is :
options: The force of metaphors that blunts description.
The mind that goes astray toward the original.
The metaphysical poets’ tendency to saunter away.
The metaphysical insistence on the particular than the general.
items.explanation: Johnson faults the metaphysicals for dwelling on small particulars and so losing the 'grandeur of generality'.

items.title: Q47 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)

items.stem:
Herr God, Herr Lucifer

The fairy-tale of a girl in the woods

items.title: Q48 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)

(ii) Esther Johnson
(iii) Rebecca Dingley
(iv) Lady Mary Montagu
The right combination according to the code is :
items.explanation: The Journal to Stella was addressed to Esther Johnson (Stella) and her companion Rebecca Dingley.

items.title: Q49 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Parallel 19th-C Tracks: American Renaissance, Realism & Early Indian English · Unit II: Poetry · Emily Dickinson

items.explanation: Dickinson's poem begins 'After great pain, a formal feeling comes –'.

a war memoir by Edmund Blunden
a war poem by Yevgeny Yevtushenko

items.explanation: Tom's poaching adventures get the gamekeeper Black George into trouble in Fielding's Tom Jones.

items.explanation: The narrator of The Unfortunate Traveller (1594) is Jack Wilton, a roguish page in Henry VIII's army.

Match the author with the title :
(Author) (Title)

items.explanation: Paton wrote Cry, the Beloved Country, Ngugi A Grain of Wheat, Teju Cole Open City, and Soyinka The Interpreters.

items.title: Q56 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · George Orwell
items.stem:
The “grammar bullies” – you read them in places like the New York Times – and they tell you what is correct.
You must never use “hopefully”. “Hopefully, we will be going there on Thursday.” That is incorrect and wrong and you are basically an ignorant pig if you say it.
This is judgementalism. The game that is being played there is a game of social class. It has nothing do with the morality of writing and speaking and thinking clearly, of which George Orwell, for instance, talked so well.
To which famous essay of Orwell does the author refer here ?
items.explanation: Orwell's 'Politics and the English Language' (1946) is his famous essay on writing and thinking clearly.

items.title: Q57 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)

items.meta: Parallel Modernist Tracks: American Modernism, Harlem Renaissance & Indian Gandhian Era · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Lorraine Hansberry, Langston Hughes

items.explanation: The play's title and epigraph come from Langston Hughes's 'Harlem', which asks 'What happens to a dream deferred?'

items.title: Q59 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)

A minimal pidgin that emerged during colonial times in the Madras Presidency.
A dialect of English spoken by the descendants of Anglo-Indians.
A pidgin, also called “Kitchen English” spoken by South Asians in Europe.
items.explanation: Butler English is a minimal pidgin used by domestic servants, which arose in colonial South India (Madras Presidency).

items.title: Q61 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)

items.title: Q63 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)

items.explanation: The novel was serialised in 1864 in the Indian Field but Bankim did not publish it as a book soon after, so that statement is false.

items.title: Q64 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Matthew Arnold
items.stem: In his essay “The Function of Criticism at the Present Time” (1864) Matthew Arnold contended that
options: Critical power should be ranked higher than creative power
Creative power should be ranked higher than critical power
Creative and critical powers should be ranked equally
Creative and critical powers are not comparable in any way
items.explanation: Arnold says the creative power is higher than the critical, but criticism prepares the ground for great creative work.

items.title: Q65 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Charles Dickens
items.stem: Identify the character, a black-eyed dwarf who “constantly revealed a few discoloured fangs that were yet scattered in his mouth, and gave him the aspect of a panting dog”.
options: Daniel Quilp in The Old Curiosity Shop
items.explanation: This is the grotesque dwarf Daniel Quilp in Dickens's The Old Curiosity Shop.

items.title: Q66 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)

The right combination according to the code is :

items.title: Q68 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)

items.stem:
The following lines are W.B. Yeats’s metaphor for an old man :
A tattered coat upon a stick, unless
Soul clap its hands and sing, and louder sing
For every tatter in its mortal dress.
Here, the aged man is ________, and his “soul ... in its mortal dress,” is ________.
items.explanation: The subject being described (the aged man) is the tenor, and the image used to describe it is the vehicle. Marked doubtful because the second blank is open to argument.

items.title: Q69 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)

items.explanation: In Greene's The Human Factor (1978) Maurice Castle, a double agent, uses book codes with classic novels. Marked doubtful.

items.explanation: Miss Prism says this to Cecily about her political economy lessons in The Importance of Being Earnest.

items.title: Q71 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
“What is honour ? A word. What is that word honour ? Air. A trim reckoning ! Who hath it ? He that died o’ Wednesday. Doth he feel it ? No. Doth he hear it ? No. Is it insensible, then ? Yea, to the dead. But will it not live with the living ? No. Why ? Detraction will not suffer it. — therefore, I’ll none of it: Honour is a mere scutcheon; and so ends my catechism.”
Which character in the following Shakespeare’s dramas made this statement about honour ?
options: Claudius in Hamlet, the Prince of Denmark
Falstaff in King Henry IV-Part I
Hotspur in King Henry IV-Part I
Hamlet in Hamlet, the Prince of Denmark
items.explanation: Falstaff says this 'catechism' on honour before the Battle of Shrewsbury in Henry IV, Part 1 (Act 5, Scene 1).

items.title: Q72 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)

Chronicles of a Riot Foretold, Shame

items.title: Q75 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)

a quack in the Indian outback.

items.title: Q76 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)

items.title: Q78 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: The Norman Conquest was a significant landmark in English history. What French did the Normans speak and what was it known as?

They spoke Norman French (Anglo-Norman). Theirs was certainly not the standard French.
They spoke normal French, rather distinct from Anglo-Norman, another standard language.
They spoke a dialectal French (also called Anglo-Frisian), somewhat closer to the Parisian.

Mattie Jane Jackson – The Story of Mattie J. Jackson
Elizabeth – Memoir of Old Elizabeth, a Coloured Woman

items.title: Q82 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)

items.stem: Which of the following had the alternative title Things as They Are?
options: Horace Walpole’s The Castle of Otranto

items.title: Q83 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Caroline & Commonwealth / Puritan Interregnum · Unit II: Poetry · Andrew Marvell
items.stem: What is the delicate balancing act of Andrew Marvell’s “Horatian Ode” ?
options: Praising Roman virtues while endorsing Christian beliefs.
Praising feminine virtues while mocking the fixation on chastity.
Celebrating Cromwell’s victories while inviting sympathy for the executed King.
Celebrating the Restoration while regretting the frivolity of the new regime.

items.title: Q84 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)

items.title: Q85 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Allen Tate
items.stem: Allen Tate once made a useful distinction between structure and texture. The distinction referred to
options: the rhetorical, stylistic, metaphorical and other devices, and the main line of a narrative, argument, etc., respectively.
objects and materials on which a narrative casts light, and the devices employed to enlighten them respectively.
the main line of a narrative, argument, etc., and the rhetorical, stylistic, metaphorical and other devices respectively.
the devices employed to enlighten objects and materials in a narrative, and the objects and material themselves, respectively.

items.title: Q86 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · George Eliot

items.title: Q87 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)

items.stem:
Match the Term with the Theorist :

items.title: Q88 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII

items.title: Q89 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)

items.title: Q90 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Fanny Burney

items.title: Q91 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Early Tudor & Humanist Reformation · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Thomas More

the family gods are invoked before finalising the nuptials.
prospective husbands and wives see one another naked before agreeing to the match.
there is a community get together where prospective husbands and wives announce wedding plans endorsed by elders.

items.title: Q92 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · S.T. Coleridge

items.title: Q93 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Walter Pater
items.stem: What type of writing did Walter Pater define as “the special and opportune art of the modern world” ?
items.explanation: In 'Style' Pater calls prose 'the special and opportune art of the modern world'. Marked doubtful because the option wording is loose.

items.title: Q94 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Early Tudor & Humanist Reformation · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem: Adherents of the fourteenth century religious movement associated with vernacular preaching, translation of New Testament into English, and challenges to the authority of priests and bishops were called
items.explanation: The Lollards followed John Wycliffe and supported English Bible translation and criticism of the clergy.

items.title: Q95 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Hanif Kureishi
items.stem:
“The good thing about words,” Hanif Kureishi remarks in “Loose Tongues”, “is that their final effect is incalculable. [...] You can never know what your words might turn out to mean for yourself or for someone else; or what the world they make will be like. Anything could happen. The problem with silence is that we know exactly what it will be like.”
Kureishi, in sum, suggests :
(i) There is always some risk involved in writing/speaking.
(ii) It is better to avoid using words than to risk miscommunication.
(iii) Words being predictable, are always open to misinterpretation.
(iv) The unpredictable, in deed, is the strength of words.
Determine the correct combination according to the code :
items.explanation: Kureishi says words are risky because their effect is unpredictable, and that unpredictability is their strength. Statements (ii) and (iii) contradict the passage.

items.title: Q96 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · Lord Byron
items.stem: Which ancient Greek writer’s name is directly mentioned in Lord Byron’s poem “The Isles of Greece” ?
items.explanation: The poem begins 'The isles of Greece... Where burning Sappho loved and sung'.

items.title: Q97 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)

items.stem: Which of the following statements is true of The Way of the World ?
options: The Way of the World presents a heroine pretending to love an older man.
The Way of the World was performed and published in 1702.
The Way of the World failed on stage.
Millamant and Mirabell fail to obtain the consent of Millamant’s aunt for their marriage.
items.explanation: Congreve's The Way of the World (1700) was coolly received at its first performances. It was published in 1700 and the couple do win Lady Wishfort's consent. Marked doubtful.

items.title: Q98 · Dec 2018 (Set 2)
items.meta: Edwardian, Georgian & Irish Literary Revival · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Henrik Ibsen
items.stem:
The following is an extract from a famous play. Read it carefully to answer questions that follow.
MAID : [From the hall doorway.] Ma’am, a lady to see you –
NORA : All right, let her come in.
[... The MAID shows in MRS. LINDE, dressed in travelling clothes, and shuts the door after her.]
MRS. LINDE : [In a dispirited and somewhat hesitant voice.] Hello, Nora.
NORA : [Uncertain.] Hello –
MRS. LINDE : You don’t recognize me.
NORA : No, I don’t know – but wait, I think – [Exclaiming.] What ! What ! Is it really you ?
MRS. LINDE : Yes, It’s me.
NORA : Kristine ! To think I didn’t recognize you. But then, how could I ? [More quietly.] How you’ve changed, Kristine !
MRS. LINDE : Yes, no doubt I have. In nine – ten long years.
NORA : It is so long since we met ! Yes, it’s all of that. Oh, these last eight years have been a happy time, believe me. And so now you’ve come in to town, too. Made the long trip in the winter. That took courage.
MRS. LINDE : I just got here by ship this morning.
NORA : To enjoy yourself over Christmas, of course. Oh, how lovely ! Yes, enjoy ourselves, we’ll do that. But take your coat off. You’re not still cold ? [Helping her.] There now, let’s get cozy here by the stove. No, the easy chair there ! I’ll take the rocker here. [Seizing her hands.] Yes, now you have your old look again; it was only in that first moment. You’re a bit more pale, Kristine – and maybe a bit thinner.
MRS. LINDE : And much, much older, Nora.
NORA : Yes, perhaps a bit older; a tiny, tiny bit; not much at all. [Stopping short, suddenly serious.] Oh, but thoughtless me, to sit here, chattering away. Sweet, good Kristine, can you forgive me ?
MRS. LINDE : What do you mean, Nora ?
NORA : [Softly.] Poor Kristine, you’ve become a widow.
MRS. LINDE : Yes, three years ago.
NORA : Oh, I knew it, of course; I read it in the papers. Oh, Kristine, you must believe me; I often thought of writing you then, but kept postponing it, and something always interfered.
MRS. LINDE : Nora, dear, I understand completely.
NORA : No, it was awful of me, Kristine. You poor thing, how much you have gone through. And he left you nothing ?
MRS. LINDE : No.
NORA : And no children ?
MRS. LINDE : No.
NORA : Nothing at all, then ?
MRS. LINDE : Not even a sense of loss to feed on.
NORA : [Looking incredulously at her.] But Kristine, how could that be ?
MRS. LINDE : [Smiling wearily and smoothing her hair.] Oh, sometimes it happens, Nora.
NORA : So completely alone. How terribly hard that must be for you. I have three lovely children. You can’t see them now; they’re out with the maid.
[...]

Which of the following descriptions best applies to the above extract ?
options: A meeting of two friends – one married, the other unmarried after a gap of years.
Friends comparing notes and counting losses in a meeting sudden and unanticipated.
A chance meeting between old friends which leaves one puzzling over the inexplicable losses the other suffered.
The sense of loss inevitable with the passage of time and the imperceptible dissolution of the conventional marriage.
items.explanation: Nora is a happily married mother and Kristine is a widow, so it is a reunion of two old friends in very different situations.

“Not even a sense of loss to feed on” implies that

items.explanation: Kristine means her marriage left her with no grief to hold on to, so her break from the past is complete. Marked doubtful.
